Romano-Wolf stepdown p-values

Source: R/effects.R
trop_stepdown.Rd

trop_stepdown() adjusts the p-values of many tests for multiple testing. The tests can be for many outcomes, or for many groups of one outcome. The function uses the stepdown method of Romano and Wolf (2005). It controls the probability of one or more false rejections. The method uses the joint bootstrap distribution of all estimates. Thus, all estimates must have the same bootstrap draws.

Usage

trop_stepdown(x)

# S3 method for class 'trop_stepdown'
print(x, digits = 4L, ...)

Arguments

x

A trop object, a trop_effects object with a bootstrap, or a list of such objects. Use a named list to name the tests. All objects must have the same bootstrap draws. Refer to the section Joint draws. The result of trop_contrast() is also a trop_effects object.

digits

The number of significant digits to show.

...

Not used.

Value

A data frame of class trop_stepdown with one row for each estimate and with the columns name, estimate, std.error, t, p_raw, and p_adj. The column p_raw is the bootstrap p-value of one test, and p_adj is the adjusted p-value. An estimate with no standard error has no p-value. The attribute n_draws is the number of draws that the function uses, and n_boot is the number of draws.

Details

For each estimate, the function calculates the statistic \(t = \hat\theta / se\), where the standard error is the standard deviation of the draws. The null hypothesis is that the effect is 0. The statistics of the draws are the absolute values of the centered draws divided by the standard errors. The function sorts the estimates by \(|t|\). In each step, it compares \(|t|\) with the largest statistic of the draws over the estimates that remain.

The p-value is (1 + the number of draws with a value that is equal or larger) / (the number of draws + 1). An adjusted p-value is never smaller than the adjusted p-value of an estimate with a larger \(|t|\).

The function uses only the draws that have a value for all estimates. It gives a warning message if some draws do not have a value for all estimates. The print method shows the number of draws that it uses. The result is not exact if the number of draws is small.

Joint draws

Draw b of each object must use the same units. Give the same boot_rows from trop_boot_rows() to each trop() and trop_effects() call. Use the same order of the units in each panel.

If each object has valid unit names, the function compares the units of each draw. A valid name is not NA, and each unit has a different name. A fit of trop() always has valid names. A fit of trop_matrix() has the row names of Y. If no object has unit names, the function compares only the row numbers.

If only some objects have valid names, draw b of all objects must have the same row numbers. The objects with valid names must also have the same units. Then the function gives a warning.

References

Romano, J. P., and Wolf, M. (2005). Stepwise Multiple Testing as Formalized Data Snooping. Econometrica, 73(4), 1237-1282.

See also

trop_boot_rows(), trop_effects(), trop_contrast()

Examples

sim <- trop_simulate(n_units = 20, n_periods = 12, n_treated = 5,
                     n_post = 3, effect = 1, seed = 1)
W <- tapply(sim$d, list(sim$unit, sim$time), sum)
rows <- trop_boot_rows(W, n_boot = 40, seed = 1)
fit <- trop(sim, "y", "d", "unit", "time",
            lambda = c(time = 0.2, unit = 0.5, nn = 0.5),
            boot_rows = rows, control = trop_control(threads = 1))
trop_stepdown(trop_effects(fit, by = "event_time"))
#> Romano-Wolf stepdown p-values
#>  name estimate std.error        t   p_raw   p_adj
#>     0  1.41712    0.3613  3.92245 0.02439 0.02439
#>     1  1.97684    0.4882  4.04929 0.02439 0.02439
#>     2 -0.03763    0.3831 -0.09821 0.87805 0.87805
#> Draws: 40 of 40 have a value for all estimates. The p-values use these draws.
